messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Vignette:
Rangi Tūhoe is a 45-year-old Māori man, born in Auckland and living in the United States for the past twelve years, where he built a reputation as a respected chef at a mid-range Pacific fusion restaurant in Portland. He came to his first session recently divorced, visibly exhausted, and speaking with the careful precision of someone who had rehearsed what he was willing to say. The event he disclosed had occurred fourteen months earlier, when a male colleague — someone Rangi had trusted and occasionally shared late-night closing shifts with — sexually assaulted him in the restaurant's dry-storage room after the rest of the staff had gone home for the night. The assault was prolonged, and it took place in a space surrounded by the smells and textures of his working life: the close air of a sealed room, the hard edge of a metal shelving unit, the particular quality of silence in a kitchen after service ends. Rangi had not reported it. He told himself, at first, that he was not sure exactly what had happened.

That uncertainty has not resolved. When Rangi tries to reconstruct the night, the sequence refuses to hold still. He can access pieces — a sound, a position, a moment of realisation — but they arrive out of order and without the connective tissue that would make them a coherent story. He finds, too, that when a memory begins to gather detail and approach something complete, something in him moves to interrupt it, to redirect attention elsewhere before the full picture can form. He described this in session not as relief but as a kind of compulsion he does not entirely control. At the same time, and paradoxically, he can speak about the event in general terms with a fluency that initially surprised his intake clinician — summarising facts, naming the perpetrator, describing the location — as though the verbal account and the felt memory belong to entirely different registers of experience.

What has accumulated in the months since is a portrait of a man who has come to understand himself as fundamentally changed and, in his own framing, ruined. Rangi had defined himself through his craft for two decades. Cooking was not merely his occupation; it was the organising principle of his identity, his connection to his Māori heritage through hāngī technique and indigenous ingredients, and the source of his self-respect after his marriage ended five years ago. He now believes he is no longer capable of being that person. He stands at the pass during service and feels, as he put it, like a stranger wearing his own hands. The precision that once came naturally — the timing, the instinct, the authority over his kitchen — feels borrowed and provisional, as though it might be revoked at any moment.

The dry-storage room remains the most immediate difficulty. Rangi has not entered it since the assault. He reorganised his prep schedule so that junior staff retrieve everything he needs, and he has offered no explanation to his team. The kitchen — once an extension of his body — now contains a locked geography. His colleagues have noticed a change in him, and two have quietly asked if he is all right. He deflects these questions with the ease of someone who has practised deflection, but each inquiry costs him something.

Beneath his composure, Rangi carries a persistent sense of contamination that he struggles to articulate without visible distress. He described feeling, at certain moments, as though something has settled into his skin that cannot be washed away — a feeling that intensifies after shifts when he has been physically close to other staff, or when he catches his reflection in the stainless steel surfaces that line his kitchen. He does not use the word shame directly, but what he describes is the lived texture of it: the belief that what happened to him has left a mark that others could perceive if they looked carefully enough.

He came to therapy, he said, because his ex-wife — with whom he remains in contact — told him she was worried he was disappearing. He did not disagree with her. What he most fears, sitting in the intake chair, is that the person he was before the assault no longer exists to be recovered. What he most hopes, though he offered this quietly and without much conviction, is that he might be wrong about that.
